title: Austria's golden age, and everyone catching up
p1: Each band is one nation's share of the podium places in a season. At the end of the 2000s Austria were close to unbeatable, with Gregor Schlierenzauer and Thomas Morgenstern winning week after week. It didn't last. Jumpers retired, other teams caught up and the lead moved around – Slovenia, Norway, Japan. By 2021 an Austrian on the podium was a rare sight, which makes the 2025 comeback even more of a surprise.

title: Japan first, Slovenia now
p1: Each band is one nation's share of the podium places in a season. When the women's World Cup started, Japan and Sara Takanashi set the pace and led every season from 2013 to 2017. Since then it's moved around – Norway, Germany and Austria have all had a turn – and Slovenia have come out on top in four of the last five.

title: Some winters belong to one jumper
p1: Bars show the share of a season's events won by its best jumper. Adam Malysz in 2000/01, Gregor Schlierenzauer in 2008/09 and Peter Prevc in 2015/16 each won around half. The men's field has still always been fairly open though – the strip underneath shows 6 to 15 different winners every season.

title: From one-woman seasons to an open field
p1: Bars show the share of a season's events won by its best jumper. Sara Takanashi lost only three times in 2013/14, and Nika Prevc won fifteen events in 2024/25. Now look at the strip underneath: only a handful of different winners a season early on, eight to ten now.

title: Most World Cup wins, 2001–2025
p1: Most of these empires were built around one jumper. Gregor Schlierenzauer won his first World Cup event at 16 and led Austria for a decade; Stefan Kraft has carried them since.

title: Most World Cup wins, 2012–2025
p1: Sara Takanashi has won more World Cup events than any ski jumper, man or woman – more than twice as many as the next best, Norway's Maren Lundby.

title: The podium is getting older
p1: In the early 2000s teenagers were regulars on the podium. Now the winners tend to be in their late twenties. And then there's Noriaki Kasai, who won in Ruka in November 2014 aged 42.

title: A young sport growing up
p1: The first women's podiums were full of teenagers – Takanashi was winning before she could drive. The sport has grown up since, and Eva Pinkelnig was still winning in her mid-thirties.

title: Home advantage? Mostly a myth
p1: For most nations a home crowd makes little difference, and Austria's and Poland's men actually do worse at home. Slovenia at Planica is the exception – their podium rate more than doubles.

title: Home advantage? Depends who you ask
p1: Norway's and Austria's women do a little better on home snow; Germany's, Japan's and Slovenia's do worse. No real pattern.

title: Longest jump of each season (m)
p1: On the big ski-flying hills the longest jump sat around 250 m for about ten years, until Domen Prevc's world record at Planica in 2025.

title: Longest jump of each season (m)
p1: Women weren't allowed on a World Cup ski-flying hill until March 2024. First time out they went almost 80 m further than any woman had in a World Cup before.

title: SO, WHO RULES THE SKIES?
p1: Nobody for long. Men's empires form around one or two great jumpers and fade when those jumpers do, the winners are getting older, and jumping at home doesn't guarantee anything. And they keep going further.

title: SO, WHO RULES THE SKIES?
p1: The women's World Cup is still young and it's opening up quickly – from one jumper winning almost every week to eight or ten winners a season, and from normal hills to 230 m flights. Nobody owns it yet.
